Chapter 10: Crime and Forgiveness—When Children Break the Law
Sometimes, the differences that shake a family have nothing to do with where a child was born, or who their parents are. Instead, it’s about choices. Imagine getting that call—the kind that makes the world stop. Your child’s been arrested, accused of something you never imagined. It’s a shock that cuts deep, leaving you questioning everything you thought you knew about your family, and even yourself.
One mother shared what it was like the night police knocked on her door. Her son, who she remembered as a quiet, thoughtful kid, had been caught stealing. The shame? It was crushing. Suddenly, friends stopped reaching out. Neighbors started whispering. Pretty soon, the whole family just pulled back into silence.
The road through the criminal justice system is confusing and, honestly, pretty brutal. Parents find themselves thrown into a world of legal terms and courtrooms, learning fast how to stand up for their child. Some start to look inward, wondering if they missed warning signs or made mistakes. Others get angry at a system that can seem more focused on punishment than on understanding what really happened.
Juvenile justice doesn’t come with simple solutions. Some kids are stuck in tough cycles—poverty, trauma, addiction. And then, there are those who make one bad decision that changes everything. The line between victim and perpetrator can get blurry, leaving families struggling to understand how things went so wrong.
Forgiveness, if it comes at all, doesn’t come easy. Some parents decide they just can’t deal with the pain and step away. But others, they hold on—writing letters, visiting, hoping for a second chance, even when that hope feels fragile. Outside the family, forgiveness is even harder to find. There’s a lot of judgment, and it can feel like you’re completely alone.
But here’s the thing—over time, some families do find a way forward. They start to separate the mistake from the person, holding onto love even when trust has taken a hit. It’s a slow process, full of setbacks and, every now and then, small steps forward.
And maybe the most important lesson? You’re not defined by your worst moment. There is room for change, for forgiveness, for healing. It’s real, even if it isn’t simple or fast.
